{"markdown":"# Research Loop: Delegate the Experiment Loop, Keep the Scientific Judgment

As of: 2026-10-15

The useful development in the supplied evidence is a more concrete division of research work. Agents can execute bounded changes, evaluate candidates and preserve experiment histories; humans still define what counts as progress and decide what deserves further validation. Our interpretation is that these reports support bounded delegation, with scientific responsibility remaining with the researcher. For students, the practical question is which parts of an experiment can be delegated while keeping its reasoning and results inspectable. <!-- claim_id: 01-c6 -->

The protein-language-model account by Li and Lu makes that boundary explicit. They report long-range contact precision rising from 28.2% to 36.6% P@L at a matched 48.4B-token budget, starting from the ESMC recipe. A human chose which recipes to scale up. That gate belongs in any description of the result: the authors report a human-guided search, and the improvement concerns a proxy metric for downstream protein folding. It does not establish fully autonomous discovery or a general improvement across scientific tasks. [Original account](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/). <!-- claim_id: 01-c1 -->

The methodological lesson is that the objective must precede the search. Li and Lu’s proposed framework fixes the scientific outcome, constrains what the agent may change and calls for larger-budget retraining against the baseline. Our recommendation for a student project follows that separation: write down the outcome you actually care about before asking an agent to optimize anything, and reserve the decision to scale a candidate for a deliberate review. A promising search result should become a candidate for validation, rather than the experiment’s final conclusion. [Research framework](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/). <!-- claim_id: 01-c6 -->

Agora adds a complementary capability: a reusable record of how an experiment developed. Its authors describe agents selecting a parent, checking out its exact Git commit, changing code, evaluating it and committing the materials needed for reproduction. The recent report concerns a run from April 26 to May 8; publication within this evidence window should not be confused with recent execution. What the report contributes here is an account of an operational research loop whose successive changes have explicit ancestry. [Agora paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094). <!-- claim_id: 01-c2 -->

That history also includes unsuccessful attempts, which later workers reportedly consulted when choosing directions. Read alongside the protein account, this suggests a useful division between execution and memory: delegate bounded trials, but require the agent to preserve why a candidate was tried, what changed and what happened—including failure. This is our practical inference from the reports. The value for a student is an inspectable basis for deciding what to try next, rather than merely receiving a winning configuration without its history. [Agora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094); [protein research framework](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/). <!-- claim_id: 01-c6 -->

An extensive history does not, however, establish independent validation. Agora’s authors report human interventions during the run, selection of every component on the same 200-text development evaluator and no fresh author rerun of the winning method. Their primary result rests on archived evaluator output, supported by agent-reported reproductions across hardware. Our reading is that this supports scrutiny of the recorded process while leaving an important gap: repeated selection and reproduction within that process do not establish that the selected method succeeds on an independent evaluation. [Methods and verification account](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094). <!-- claim_id: 01-c3 -->

Periodic Labs offers a physical-laboratory contrast. In the supplied provisional transcript, its founders describe campaign guidance becoming a mixture of human and AI work, while characterization shifted substantially toward AI assistance. This is testimony about their workflow, not a controlled measurement of productivity. The supplied segment contains neither inspectable execution logs nor measurements that would establish a transferable gain. [Latent Space podcast, 1:04:24–1:05:04](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic). <!-- claim_id: 01-c4 -->

The founders also describe full autonomy as a non-goal, placing automation in service of obtaining useful data. Elsewhere, they discuss bringing their tools to industry partners. Their account therefore supplies a commercially interested operational perspective, not independent corroboration of the computational results. Its relevance is the stated allocation of work around experimental needs. [Podcast, 50:46–51:39 and 1:15:06–1:16:53](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic). <!-- claim_id: 01-c5 -->

Together, these sources suggest connecting execution, memory and human judgment without collapsing them into a claim of hands-free science. They describe different projects, not independent replications of one result, and do not establish portable speed or cost gains. For your next small computational experiment, fix the objective, bound the permitted changes, preserve unsuccessful trials and decide explicitly which candidates merit larger validation runs. That delegation boundary is our synthesis; the responsibility for accepting the result remains yours. <!-- claim_id: 01-c1, 01-c3, 01-c4, 01-c5, 01-c6 -->

## References

- Li and Lu. [Hill-Climbing a Protein Language Model: A Taste of Autoresearch for Scientific Discovery](https://jojoml.github.io/blog/2026/nanoproteinlm-agenticls/). September 30, 2026.
- [Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18094). September 16, 2026.
- Latent Space. [Synthesis Superintelligence: from Semiconductors to Superconductors — Periodic Labs’ Liam Fedus and Ekin Dogus Cubuk](https://www.latent.space/p/periodic). October 8, 2026. Cited podcast segments: 50:46–51:39; 1:04:24–1:05:04; 1:15:06–1:16:53. Supplied transcript is provisional.
